SEPARATE TWO-CENTRE EXPERIMENT · EXPLORATORY

When can the court leave while farming continues?

Accounts and decisions

Two sites each have rural households, ordinary core residents, developed land, water condition, monuments and finite grain stores. A fixed elite population starts 80% at the old centre. Ordinary households can grow or shrink. Elite households and workers transfer between sites under separate rules. Farmers remain in place by assumption. Neither centre has a calibrated geography.

Each site produces harvest = land × 1.5 × 5^0.227 × (0.65 + 0.35 × water condition) × climate × available farm labour. The coordination exponent comes from the provisioning paper; its causal use is an Atlas assumption. The other coefficients are illustrative. Collection is 20% of harvest multiplied by (0.3 + 0.7 × local elite share). Transport loses 8% of collection. Retained harvest feeds farmers, then funds optional local upkeep; the rest is recorded as other household use. Central receipts pay urban food, ritual, maintenance, reserves, reclamation and construction. Existing stores lose 4% per step and meet food shortfalls before investment. All uses enter the ledger.

Utility = 0.65 × core food coverage + 0.35 × water condition − 2 × hunger. The second-centre opportunity multiplies its utility. Moving there loses (1 − portability) × 0.5 × old water condition in place-bound asset value. Elites move only when the utility gap exceeds the moving hurdle, at a maximum 8% of origin elites per step. The hurdle is a utility threshold, not a grain expense. Portability discounts an asset-value index, without a private wealth ledger.

Workers move independently according to provisioning and changing elite demand, at up to 2.5% per step. Moving conserves people; demographic change is accounted for separately. Local farm surpluses can sustain repairs without elite participation. New construction creates recurring obligations, so departure can reduce future commitments as well as receipts.

Time is elapsed model years. Droughts at years 150–174 and 190–204 impose 62% conditions at the old centre and 85% at the second. The southern advantage is an imposed scenario, not an inferred historical climate difference. Water is a single condition index, with no hydraulic network or flood cascade.

9,216 simulated histories

Grid: outside opportunity 0.8, 1.2, 1.6; moving hurdle 0.05, 0.25, 0.5; portability 0.25, 0.75; local repair 0, 0.75; stable or drought climate; 32 matched weather seeds. These 2,304 settings each run four mobility rules: elites and workers, neither, elites only, workers only. Seeds vary small weather noise. The grid is a sensitivity design, not a historical probability distribution.

Persistent departure means fewer than 40% of all elites at the old centre for ten consecutive steps. Retention is final population divided by its own peak. The table reports means across the declared grid. Farming persistence depends on the exclusion of rural relocation.

At outside opportunity 1.2 with drought, persistent departure occurs in 128/128 settings at moving hurdle 0.05, 14/128 at 0.25, and 0/128 at 0.5. With portability 0.75 it occurs in 78/192 settings, compared with 64/192 at portability 0.25. These counts vary the other declared grid dimensions while matching weather seeds.

The complication: leaving can help water maintenance

At opportunity 1.6 with drought, average final old water condition is 59.8% with both groups mobile, 42.5% with neither mobile, 41.7% with elites only, and 52.2% with workers only. Elite departure and worker departure have different effects. Moving workers reduces the central food bill, while lower construction can reduce recurring obligations. Local repairs can continue. The model therefore does not support an automatic chain from elite exit to hydraulic collapse.

The old residential core retains about 70.7% of its own peak in this high-opportunity drought group. This is a partial contraction, not an emptied city. The farming stock remains high partly because rural households cannot migrate. These outcomes test this implementation, with utilities, collection rules, movement rates, fixed elite numbers and second-centre advantages still assumed.

Food accounting and migrant conservation passed 10⁻¹⁰ tolerances for the main and blocked-movement comparisons. Automated checks also cover all four movement rules. Arithmetic checks are distinct from historical validation.

Sources and Atlas contribution

Hall, Penny and Hamilton (2018) document settlement continuing at Koh Ker after court departure. Penny and colleagues (2019) constrain gradual change in Angkor Thom. Penny and Beach (2021) discuss mobility and heterogeneous responses. They provide evidence and questions, not this utility model.
